questions.stem: Imagine you are building a software system that frequently merges large priority queues. According to the text, why would you choose binomial heaps over standard binary heaps?
options: Binary heap UNION operations run in worst-case time O(lg n), whereas binomial heaps perform UNION in Theta(1) time.
Binary heap UNION operations take Theta(n) time in the worst case, whereas binomial heaps can merge two heaps of total size n in O(lg n) time.
Binary heaps do not support the UNION operation at all, making binomial heaps the only choice for mergeable priority queues.
Binary heaps perform poorly on MINIMUM operations, taking O(lg n) time compared to the binomial heap's Theta(1) time.
questions.explanation: The text states that concatenating two arrays for binary heaps and running MIN-HEAPIFY takes Theta(n) time, whereas a binomial heap performs UNION in O(lg n) time.

questions.stem: According to Lemma 19.1, what is the exact number of nodes located at depth i in a binomial tree Bk?
options: Exactly 2^i nodes
Exactly k - i nodes
Exactly the binomial coefficient (k choose i) nodes
Exactly 2^(k - i) nodes
questions.explanation: Lemma 19.1 explicitly states that there are exactly (k choose i) nodes at depth i for i = 0, 1, ..., k.

questions.stem: This sounds plausible, but is it true? True or False: In a binomial heap with 13 nodes, it is possible to have two separate binomial trees of degree 2 (B2) as long as both strictly obey the min-heap property.
options: True, as long as both trees are min-heap-ordered, the binomial heap is valid.
False, a binomial heap can have at most one binomial tree whose root has degree k for any nonnegative integer k.
questions.explanation: The second binomial-heap property dictates that for any nonnegative integer k, there is at most one binomial tree in the heap whose root has degree k.

questions.stem: How are binomial trees within a binomial heap represented in memory to efficiently support operations?
options: Each node contains pointers to its parent, its leftmost child, and its immediate right sibling.
Each node is stored in a standard contiguous array utilizing implicit index calculations similar to a binary heap.
Each node contains a dynamic array of pointers to all of its children, plus a parent pointer.
Each node contains pointers to its parent, its left sibling, and its right sibling, forming a doubly linked list of children.
questions.explanation: The text explains that binomial trees are stored in the 'left-child, right-sibling' representation, containing pointers p[x] to the parent, child[x] to the leftmost child, and sibling[x] to the right sibling.

questions.stem: When uniting two binomial heaps, the BINOMIAL-LINK procedure makes one Bk-1 tree the child of another to form a Bk tree. What is the time complexity of this specific linking procedure?
options: O(lg n), because it must update the sibling pointers of all existing children to append the new node.
O(k), because it needs to update the degree field of all children in the tree.
O(1), because the left-child, right-sibling representation allows making a node the new head of a linked list in constant time.
O(lg n), because it must bubble the newly linked node down to maintain the min-heap property.
questions.explanation: The text states that BINOMIAL-LINK makes node y the new head of the linked list of node z's children in O(1) time.

questions.stem: During the while loop of BINOMIAL-HEAP-UNION, what action is taken in 'Case 2', where the current root (x), the next root (next-x), and the sibling of the next root all have the exact same degree?
options: The procedure links x and next-x immediately, creating a root of higher degree.
The pointers are simply marched one position farther down the root list without linking any roots in this iteration.
The procedure stops and throws an error, because a valid binomial heap operation should never encounter three roots of the same degree.
The procedure links next-x and its sibling, removing the sibling from the root list.
questions.explanation: In Case 2, when x is the first of three roots of equal degree, the algorithm just marches the pointers one position farther down the list to defer the linking to the next iteration.

questions.stem: True or False: To perform BINOMIAL-HEAP-EXTRACT-MIN, the algorithm extracts the root with the minimum key, reverses the order of the linked list of that root's children to form a new binomial heap, and then unites this new heap with the remaining original heap.
options: True, reversing the children creates a valid binomial heap H' that is then united with the original heap H.
False, the children of the extracted root are inserted one by one back into the original heap using BINOMIAL-HEAP-INSERT.
questions.explanation: BINOMIAL-HEAP-EXTRACT-MIN explicitly removes the minimum root, reverses the linked list of its children to form a new heap H', and calls BINOMIAL-HEAP-UNION on H and H'.

questions.stem: How does the BINOMIAL-HEAP-DECREASE-KEY procedure ensure that the min-heap property is maintained after a node's key is reduced to a new value?
options: It 'bubbles down' the key by exchanging it with the smallest of its children until it is less than or equal to all of its children.
It removes the node from the heap entirely and inserts a new node with the decreased key using BINOMIAL-HEAP-INSERT.
It 'bubbles up' the key by repeatedly exchanging it with its parent's key until it is greater than or equal to its parent's key or it becomes a root.
It links the node directly to the root list, treating it as a new binomial tree of degree zero.
questions.explanation: The text explains that BINOMIAL-HEAP-DECREASE-KEY works similarly to a binary min-heap by 'bubbling up' the key, exchanging it with its parent until min-heap ordering is restored.

questions.stem: You are tasked with implementing the DELETE operation to remove a specific node x from a binomial heap. According to the text, what is the correct sequence of operations to accomplish this in O(lg n) time?
options: Call BINOMIAL-HEAP-EXTRACT-MIN repeatedly until node x is returned, then rebuild the heap.
Replace node x's key with the key of the last node in the heap, then delete the last node and bubble down.
Unlink node x from its parent and append all of x's children directly to the root list.
Decrease the key of node x to negative infinity and then call BINOMIAL-HEAP-EXTRACT-MIN.
questions.explanation: BINOMIAL-HEAP-DELETE makes node x have the unique minimum key by decreasing it to negative infinity, bubbling it up to a root, and then extracting it via BINOMIAL-HEAP-EXTRACT-MIN.

questions.stem: A common misconception is that Fibonacci heaps are strictly better than binomial heaps in every regard. Based on the chapter introduction, why is this not entirely true?
options: True, Fibonacci heaps are strictly superior because they guarantee O(1) worst-case time bounds for every operation.
False, the impressive O(1) running times for Fibonacci heaps in Figure 19.1 are amortized time bounds, not worst-case per-operation bounds.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly notes that while Fibonacci heaps have better bounds for some operations, they are amortized time bounds, not worst-case per-operation bounds like those of binomial heaps.
